title: Dollar Slides to 10-Week Low as Cooling U.S. Data Slash Fed Rate Hike Odds
excerpt: The DXY dollar index fell to 99.294, its lowest since early June, as weak jobs, soft inflation, and shrinking retail sales leave markets pricing just a 31% chance of a September rate increase.
body:
• The DXY dollar index fell to 99.294 on Monday, its lowest level since early June, as a string of weak U.S. economic data eroded expectations for a Federal Reserve rate hike.
  • Markets now price just a 31% chance of a September rate increase, down from over 55% a week ago, after July nonfarm payrolls unexpectedly declined and inflation came in subdued.
  • The euro hit a two-month high of $1.1614 and sterling reached a three-month high of $1.3571 as interest-rate differentials shifted in their favor.
  • Traders are watching Wednesday's release of the Fed's July meeting minutes for further signals on the rate path.

The U.S. dollar fell sharply on Monday, hitting a 10-week low against a basket of major currencies as a drumbeat of weaker economic data over the past two weeks left markets increasingly convinced that the Federal Reserve will hold rates steady through the rest of the year.

The DXY dollar index dropped to 99.294 in early European trading, its lowest level since early June, according to LSEG data. The euro rose to a two-month high of $1.1614, while sterling climbed to a three-month high of $1.3571.

A Data-Driven Retreat

The dollar's slide accelerated after a series of disappointing releases. The U.S. economy unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July, according to the Labor Department, against economists' expectations for an 80,000 gain. Consumer inflation eased to 3.4% annually in July from 3.5% in June, while the Producer Price Index was flat — well below the 0.2% increase economists had forecast. On Friday, retail sales contracted 0.6% in July, far worse than the 0.1% expansion consensus.

Together, the data have dramatically reshaped rate expectations. U.S. money markets now assign just a 31% probability to a 25 basis-point hike at the Fed's September 16 meeting, down from above 55% before the August 7 jobs report, LSEG data showed. A rate rise is no longer seen as a certainty this year, with only 21 basis points of tightening priced in through December.

"Fed Chair Kevin Warsh wanted market participants to make up their mind about how the Fed should react to changing economic conditions rather be guided by forward guidance, and they are currently sending a clear signal that there is less need for the Fed to hike rates."

— Lee Hardman and Derek Halpenny, MUFG Bank

Fed Minutes in Focus

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.5% to 3.75% for the fifth consecutive meeting on July 29, though three of 12 voting policymakers dissented in favor of a hike. Chair Kevin Warsh has deliberately avoided forward guidance, placing the burden on incoming data to shape market expectations.

Traders will scrutinize the minutes of that July meeting, due Wednesday, for clues on how close the decision was to a hike and whether the committee's tone has shifted.

"Given slightly weak activity data since the July meeting, it will be hard for the market to feel fully confident again that rates will be raised, even if the minutes point to a closer call on the unchanged rates decision than most think," ING analyst Chris Turner said in a note.

Euro, Sterling Gain as Rate Paths Diverge

The dollar's weakness has been magnified by diverging rate expectations across major economies. Eurozone money markets imply an 84% chance of another European Central Bank rate hike in September, with 38 basis points of increases priced in by year-end. U.K. markets are fully pricing in a 25 basis-point Bank of England hike by December, supported by evidence that the British economy has proved more resilient than expected to the energy price shock from the Iran conflict.

Commerzbank currency analyst Volkmar Baur noted that should rate-hike bets continue to fade — the bank expects three Fed rate cuts next year — the dollar faces further downside.

Oil Prices Remain a Wildcard

Despite the broader softening in data, oil prices remain elevated as the U.S.-Iran standoff continues to disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. The White House has threatened to maintain a naval blockade of Iran indefinitely, and Houthi attacks on shipping have renewed supply concerns.

MUFG's Lee Hardman noted that U.S. equity inflows, particularly into AI-related stocks, have partially cushioned the dollar's fall. The DXY remains above its 200-day moving average of 99.200, a level that could serve as the next line of support if selling continues.

Turner expects the dollar index to "trade to the soft side all week as investors focus on higher-yielding and procyclical currencies."
